course.title: Cybersecurity — Complete Deep Security Course
course.description: A defensive, Cybersecurity-specific course progressing from fundamentals to production security, with detailed explanations, safe practicals, dedicated tasks, security testing and a complete learning-platform capstone.
course.curriculumPolicy: Module and lesson counts are determined by the security concepts required to learn the discipline properly; no fixed cross-security template is imposed.
learningOutcomes: Identify assets, threats and trust boundaries.
Secure authentication, authorization and data flows.
Integrate security into development and operations.
Respond to and learn from security failures.

modules.title: Security Foundations
modules.description: CIA triad, threat modeling, assets, threats, vulnerabilities, risk and security controls.

lessons.title: Security Foundations
lessons.description: CIA triad, threat modeling, assets, threats, vulnerabilities, risk and security controls.
learningObjectives: Test normal and malicious/invalid cases safely.

notes.text: CIA triad, threat modeling, assets, threats, vulnerabilities, risk and security controls.

Learn security foundations by first identifying the asset and trust boundary, then understanding the attack or failure mode, then applying a defense and finally testing that defense. The objective is defensive engineering, not memorizing isolated vulnerabilities.

Security Foundations is important because security failures often happen at boundaries between users, browsers, APIs, services, databases and deployment systems. Students should learn to prevent, detect and safely remediate these failures.

notes.caption: Add a defensive architecture diagram showing the trust boundary, threat and mitigation for Security Foundations.

items: Identify the asset being protected.
Identify the trust boundary and attacker capability.
Understand the failure/vulnerability mechanism.
Apply layered defensive controls.
Create a test that proves the control works.

notes.code:
Scenario: Create a threat model for a student learning platform.

Defensive workflow: identify the asset -> map the trust boundary -> define allowed behavior -> implement controls -> test negative cases -> monitor.

items: Locate the untrusted input or risky boundary.
Define what the application should allow.
Apply validation, authorization or isolation.
Verify the result with positive and negative tests.
Log the security-relevant event without exposing secrets.
Relying on client-side checks for security.
Using authentication without object-level authorization.
Logging passwords, tokens or sensitive personal data.
Fixing a symptom without identifying the trust boundary.
Skipping regression tests after a security fix.
Use defense in depth.
Enforce authorization on the server.
Keep secrets out of source code.
Prefer safe APIs and parameterized operations.
Automate security checks where practical.
Treat security findings as engineering work with owners and verification.
I can explain Security Foundations in my own words.
I can identify the affected trust boundary.
I can describe the defensive control.
I can create a negative test.
I can explain how the fix should be monitored.

lessons.title: Endpoint & Device Security
lessons.description: Device posture, updates, malware defense, secure configuration and endpoint visibility.
learningObjectives: Test normal and malicious/invalid cases safely.

notes.text: Device posture, updates, malware defense, secure configuration and endpoint visibility.

Learn endpoint & device security by first identifying the asset and trust boundary, then understanding the attack or failure mode, then applying a defense and finally testing that defense. The objective is defensive engineering, not memorizing isolated vulnerabilities.

Endpoint & Device Security is important because security failures often happen at boundaries between users, browsers, APIs, services, databases and deployment systems. Students should learn to prevent, detect and safely remediate these failures.

notes.alt: Cybersecurity Endpoint & Device Security security diagram
notes.caption: Add a defensive architecture diagram showing the trust boundary, threat and mitigation for Endpoint & Device Security.

items: Identify the asset being protected.
Identify the trust boundary and attacker capability.
Understand the failure/vulnerability mechanism.
Apply layered defensive controls.
Create a test that proves the control works.

notes.code:
Scenario: Create a baseline for developer workstations.

Defensive workflow: identify the asset -> map the trust boundary -> define allowed behavior -> implement controls -> test negative cases -> monitor.

items: Locate the untrusted input or risky boundary.
Define what the application should allow.
Apply validation, authorization or isolation.
Verify the result with positive and negative tests.
Log the security-relevant event without exposing secrets.
Relying on client-side checks for security.
Using authentication without object-level authorization.
Logging passwords, tokens or sensitive personal data.
Fixing a symptom without identifying the trust boundary.
Skipping regression tests after a security fix.
Use defense in depth.
Enforce authorization on the server.
Keep secrets out of source code.
Prefer safe APIs and parameterized operations.
Automate security checks where practical.
Treat security findings as engineering work with owners and verification.
I can explain Endpoint & Device Security in my own words.
I can identify the affected trust boundary.
I can describe the defensive control.
I can create a negative test.
I can explain how the fix should be monitored.

Business Continuity & Recovery is important because security failures often happen at boundaries between users, browsers, APIs, services, databases and deployment systems. Students should learn to prevent, detect and safely remediate these failures.

notes.code:
Scenario: Design a recovery plan for a security incident.

Defensive workflow: identify the asset -> map the trust boundary -> define allowed behavior -> implement controls -> test negative cases -> monitor.

items: Locate the untrusted input or risky boundary.
Define what the application should allow.
Apply validation, authorization or isolation.
Verify the result with positive and negative tests.
Log the security-relevant event without exposing secrets.
Relying on client-side checks for security.
Using authentication without object-level authorization.
Logging passwords, tokens or sensitive personal data.
Fixing a symptom without identifying the trust boundary.
Skipping regression tests after a security fix.
Use defense in depth.
Enforce authorization on the server.
Keep secrets out of source code.
Prefer safe APIs and parameterized operations.
Automate security checks where practical.
Treat security findings as engineering work with owners and verification.
